testCase.title: Scissor stair counted as two exits

projectContext.occupancy: Group R-2 stated by the question
projectContext.configuration: Scissor stair with entrance doors 15 feet apart

exactPassages: Stairs sharing any common wall, floor, ceiling, scissor stair assembly, or other enclosure shall be counted as one exit stairway.

3. Group R-2 occupancies. In Group R-2 occupancies, where stairs are enclosed in walls having at least a 2-hour fire resistance rating and constructed of masonry or masonry equivalent in accordance with department rules: 3.1. The exit doors to such stairs shall be placed a distance apart equal to no less than 15 feet (4572 mm); and 3.2. testCase.question: Our Group R-2 building has a scissor stair with the two stair entrance doors located 15 feet apart. Can the two stairs be counted as two separate exits?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The 15-foot separation alone is not enough. Under the general rule, stairs sharing a scissor-stair assembly are counted as one exit stairway. However, the Group R-2 exception permits the stairs to share the assembly and be counted separately when the stair enclosures and the construction separating the stairs have at least a 2-hour fire-resistance rating and are constructed of masonry or a masonry equivalent in accordance with department rules. The exit doors must also be at least 15 feet apart. Confirm the occupancy group, enclosure rating, separating construction, and material before concluding that the exception applies.

answer.conclusion: Yes—conditionally. Although stairs sharing a scissor stair assembly are generally counted as one exit stairway, the selected Group R-2 exception permits them to share a scissor stair assembly and be treated as separate stairs if all stated exception conditions are met. A 15-foot separation between the exit doors meets the exception’s minimum door-separation threshold because the required distance is “no less than 15 feet.” The stairs therefore may be counted as two separate exits only if the enclosing walls and the construction separating the stairs each have at least a 2-hour fire-resistance rating and are constructed of masonry or masonry equivalent in accordance with department rules. [Section 1007.1.1, Passages a9d92e82-7120-4cda-a571-c0f5b2ab9bb6 and 5c6e8ea8-9094-406a-8a14-8c5a233ea92c]
answer.explanation: Section 1007.1.1’s general rule counts stairs sharing a common wall, floor, ceiling, scissor stair assembly, or other enclosure as one exit stairway. It permits shared scissor stair assemblies where: (1) the stairs are enclosed by walls with at least a 2-hour fire-resistance rating and constructed of masonry or masonry equivalent under department rules; (2) the exit doors are at least 15 feet apart; and (3) the construction separating the stairs is also at least 2-hour fire-resistance-rated and masonry or masonry equivalent under department rules. testCase.title: Occupancy classification of a residential multipurpose room

exactPassages: A room or space used for assembly purposes with an occupant load of fewer than 75 persons and accessory to another occupancy shall be classified as a Group B occupancy or as part of that occupancy, except that the number of plumbing fixtures for such a room or space is permitted to be calculated in accordance with the requirements for assembly occupancies.

For areas without fixed seating, the occupant load shall be not less than that number determined by dividing the floor area under consideration by the occupant load factor assigned to the function of the space as set forth in Table 1004.1.3.

testCase.question: A 900-net-square-foot multipurpose room in an apartment building will normally contain tables and chairs and is only for residents. Does it need to be classified as Group A-3?
testCase.expectedConclusion: For an unconcentrated assembly arrangement with tables and chairs, Table 1004.1.3 uses 15 net square feet per occupant. A 900-net-square-foot room therefore has a calculated occupant load of 60 people. Because that is fewer than 75 occupants, and assuming the room is accessory to the residential occupancy, BC 303.1.3 permits it to be classified as Group B or as part of the occupancy it serves rather than as Group A. The result depends on the actual net area, furniture arrangement, intended activities, and whether the room is truly accessory to the residential use.

Calculate 900 divided by 15 as an occupant load of 60.

Avoid automatically classifying every residential amenity room as Group R-2.

forbiddenClaims: Every residential amenity room is automatically Group R-2.

answer.conclusion: Conditionally, no. If the room is an assembly-purpose space that is accessory to the apartment-building occupancy, its calculated occupant load is 60 persons (900 net square feet ÷ 15 net square feet per person). Because 60 is fewer than 75, Section 303.1.3 directs classification as Group B or as part of the occupancy to which it is accessory, rather than requiring classification as a separate assembly occupancy. The selected evidence does not itself establish the specific Group A-3 definition, but it supports use of the accessory-assembly-space rule if its conditions are verified. [Section 132, Passage ca84e062-d110-4c1a-a4d6-229e78a0ba2c; Section 2152, Passages 5d62aab7-de64-4058-abc6-032becc9cec4, 12e731e0-25b9-4cdf-81ce-e291f5a9a6e1, and 23624bc9-4af5-4c7e-a3b6-bbaf724e1cbe]
answer.explanation: The supplied occupant-load procedure applies to areas without fixed seating: divide the floor area under consideration by the Table 1004.1.3 factor assigned to the space function. The selected table entries identify “Unconcentrated (tables and chairs)” and a factor of 15 net square feet per person. Using the stated project area and normal layout: 900 net square feet ÷ 15 net square feet/person = 60 persons. Section 303.1.3 applies where an assembly-purpose room or space has an occupant load of fewer than 75 persons and is accessory to another occupancy. It then permits classification as Group B or as part of that other occupancy. That section also permits plumbing-fixture calculations for the room/space to follow assembly-occupancy requirements despite the accessory-space classification. [Section 132, Passage ca84e062-d110-4c1a-a4d6-229e78a0ba2c; Section 2152, Passages 5d62aab7-de64-4058-abc6-032becc9cec4, 12e731e0-25b9-4cdf-81ce-e291f5a9a6e1, and 23624bc9-4af5-4c7e-a3b6-bbaf724e1cbe]

testCase.title: Plumbing fixtures for an accessory assembly space

projectContext.potentialClassification: Group B under the accessory assembly provision

exactPassages: A room or space used for assembly purposes with an occupant load of fewer than 75 persons and accessory to another occupancy shall be classified as a Group B occupancy or as part of that occupancy, except that the number of plumbing fixtures for such a room or space is permitted to be calculated in accordance with the requirements for assembly occupancies.

Plumbing fixtures shall be provided for the type of occupancy and in the minimum number shown in Table 403.1. Types of occupancies not shown in Table 403.1 shall be considered individually by the commissioner. The number of occupants shall be determined by the New York City Building Code. Occupancy classification shall be determined in accordance with the New York City Building Code.

The number of fixtures for building or nonaccessory tenant space used for assembly purposes by fewer than 75 persons and classified as Group B occupancy in accordance with Section 303.1, Exception 2 of the New York City Building Code shall be permitted to be calculated in accordance with the requirements for Assembly occupancies.

To determine the occupant load of each sex, the total occupant load shall be divided in half. To determine the required number of fixtures, the fixture ratio or ratios for each fixture type shall be applied to the occupant load of each sex in accordance with Table 403.1. Fractional numbers resulting from applying the fixture ratios of Table 403.1 shall be rounded up to the next whole number. For calculations involving multiple occupancies, such fractional numbers for each occupancy shall first be summed and then rounded up to the next whole number. Fixture calculations in Group B office occupancies shall utilize the total occupant load on a given floor to determine the number of fixtures required for that floor.
Exception: The total occupant load shall not be required to be divided in half where approved statistical data indicates a distribution of the sexes of other than 50 percent of each sex.

testCase.question: If the multipurpose room is permitted to be classified as Group B because it has fewer than 75 occupants, can its required plumbing fixtures be calculated using the normal Group B fixture requirements?
testCase.expectedConclusion: Not automatically. Although an accessory assembly space with fewer than 75 occupants may be classified as Group B or as part of the occupancy it serves, the code permits the plumbing fixtures for that assembly use to be calculated using the applicable Assembly fixture requirements. The total occupant load is generally divided equally between the sexes unless approved statistical information supports another distribution. answer.conclusion: No—not as an exclusive requirement. If the multipurpose room is an assembly-use space with an occupant load of fewer than 75 persons and is accessory to another occupancy, it may be classified as Group B (or as part of the other occupancy); however, the selected Building Code provision expressly permits its plumbing-fixture count to be calculated under the Assembly-occupancy requirements. The selected Plumbing Code provision likewise permits fixtures for a qualifying sub-75-person assembly space classified as Group B to be calculated under Assembly requirements. Thus, Group B classification does not require use of the normal Group B fixture ratios for this room; Assembly fixture requirements are a permitted calculation basis. [BC §303.1.3, Passage 147efd7d-516f-4b3d-878a-2183aec70deb; PC §403.1, Passage 42667e92-8559-410c-8c96-2a4270e5f661]
answer.explanation:
PC §403.1 requires fixtures by occupancy type and the minimum counts in Table 403.1, with occupant load and occupancy classification determined under the NYC Building Code. For multiple occupancies, sum the fractional fixture results for each occupancy before rounding up. The equal sex split need not be used where approved statistical data supports a different sex distribution.
